issues.legal_issue: Income received by a company from letting shops and stalls on its land is income from property rather than business income, even when the company was formed to develop markets and provides services connected with the property.
material_facts: The company was formed, among other purposes, to promote and develop markets, bought land, and established a market with shops and stalls.
It received payments from tenants of the shops and from occupants of the stalls.
The company was required to obtain a licence and maintain sanitary and other services, which involved staff and expenditure.
Some stalls were occupied by the same occupants, while occupation of others was temporary.
issues.conclusion: The receipts from both shops and stalls were assessable as income from property, not as profits or gains of business; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 6, 9 and 10 of the Income-tax Act, 1922, the heads of income are mutually exclusive and income is classified by the source from which it arises. Income directly arising from ownership and letting of property remains property income even if the owner is a company formed to develop or manage property, provides services, or has a business purpose that may indirectly encompass the activity. The Court relied on United Commercial Bank Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Fry v. Salisbury House Estate Co. Ltd., and Commercial Properties Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax.

predicates.income_tax_source_classification_case: The proceeding concerns how receipts are classified for income-tax purposes.
predicates.shops_let_for_payment: A company received payments from tenants for letting shops on land it owned.
predicates.stalls_occupied_for_payment: A company received payments from people occupying stalls on land it owned.

issues.definition: When a proceeding classifies income for tax purposes and a company receives payments for letting shops or for occupation of its stalls, those receipts are classified as property income.
